nameStory: Leonard's Skipper was named in honor of Leonard Stejneger, a Norwegian-American ornithologist and herpetologist who worked at the Smithsonian Institution in the late 1800s and early 1900s. While Stejneger was better known for his work with birds and reptiles, having a butterfly named after him shows how interconnected the natural history community was during that era of scientific discovery.
description: Leonard's Skipper is a small, robust butterfly with a stocky build typical of the skipper family. These butterflies have a wingspan of about 1.25 to 1.75 inches across, making them smaller than a Monarch but larger than many of the tiny grass skippers. They're most notable for appearing late in the butterfly season when most other species are winding down. Like other skippers, they have large heads relative to their body size and hold their wings at distinctive angles when perched.

idTips.label: Late season timing
idTips.description: Active from August through October when most other butterflies have finished for the year - if you see a medium-sized orange skipper in September, it's likely this species

idTips.label: Wing position
idTips.description: Holds forewings upright and hindwings horizontally when perched, creating a distinctive triangular silhouette that skippers are famous for

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Flies with quick, darting movements punctuated by brief glides - much more erratic and zippy than the steady flight of larger butterflies

idTips.label: Body build
idTips.description: Chunky, moth-like body that feels substantial if you were to gently catch one - much more robust than the delicate build of swallowtails or whites

idTips.label: Nectar preferences
idTips.description: Often found on fall-blooming purple flowers like asters and thistles, where they probe deeply with their long tongues

idTips.label: Antennae shape
idTips.description: Antennae end in small hooks or clubs that curve backward slightly, unlike the straight clubs of true butterflies or the feathery antennae of moths

habitat: Look for Leonard's Skippers in open grasslands, prairies, old fields, and meadows where native grasses grow abundantly. They prefer areas with little bluestem grass and other native prairie grasses, often in spots that aren't regularly mowed. You'll also find them along woodland edges and in clearings where grasses meet wildflowers.

seasonality.spring: Adults are not active - the species exists as caterpillars feeding on grasses during this time of year.
seasonality.summer: Most of the summer is spent in the larval stage, with caterpillars quietly munching on grass blades in meadows and prairies.
seasonality.fall: Peak flight season from August through October - this is when you'll see adults nectaring on asters, thistles, and other fall wildflowers. Look for mating behavior and egg-laying on grass stems.
seasonality.winter: Overwinters as eggs or young caterpillars, completely hidden from view until the following growing season.

funFact: Leonard's Skipper is like the "night owl" of the butterfly world - while most butterfly species wrap up their adult flight period by midsummer, Leonard's Skipper doesn't even begin flying until August, making it one of the latest emerging butterflies in New England and earning it the nickname of autumn's butterfly.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other orange skippers, but the late flight season is the best clue - by the time Leonard's Skippers emerge in August, most other similar species have already finished flying for the year. If you see what looks like a Leonard's Skipper in June or July, it's probably a different species like the Indian Skipper.
contextualKnowledge: The name "skipper" comes from these butterflies' quick, skipping flight pattern that looks like they're bouncing through the air rather than flying smoothly. Despite being butterflies, skippers are sometimes considered a bridge group between true butterflies and moths due to their chunky bodies and hooked antennae.
compareHints: Leonard's Skipper differs from its close relative the Indian Skipper mainly by timing - Indian Skippers fly much earlier in the season (May through July). The American Branded Skipper is found further west and has slightly different markings on the underwing. Cobweb Skipper is much smaller and prefers sandy barrens rather than grasslands.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Indian Skipper is most similar to Leonard's Skipper but flies much earlier in the season and has slightly more orange coloring.
American Branded Skipper flies much later than Indian Skipper (which peaks in June-July) and Leonard's Skipper (July-August).
Among its Hesperia relatives, cobweb skipper is the spring flier - Indian Skipper flies in early summer and Leonard's Skipper in late summer/fall.
